```{python}
#| label: setup
import sys, warnings
sys.path.insert(0, "../slides")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

from plotstyle import setup, CL
plt = setup()

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

core = pd.read_parquet("../data/spine/core.parquet").drop(columns=["flag"])
ener = pd.read_parquet("../data/spine/angle_a_country.parquet").drop(columns=["flag"])
panel = (core.merge(ener, on=["geo", "time"])
              .dropna().sort_values(["time", "geo"]).reset_index(drop=True))

DROP = ("time", "prod_growth", "falling_behind", "falling_behind_next")
IND = [c for c in panel.select_dtypes("number").columns if c not in DROP]

Zdf = (panel[IND] - panel[IND].mean()) / panel[IND].std()
Z = Zdf.to_numpy()
U, D, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Z, full_matrices=False)
VAR = D**2 / (D**2).sum()
NOBS, NIND = Z.shape
```

# {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

:::

## Learning objectives

::: {.tight}
- Derive PCA from a constrained maximisation and see **why the answer is an eigenvector**
- State Eckart–Young and say exactly **what you lose** by truncating
- Explain why extra series **help** factor estimation and **hurt** regression
- Report a factor count from several criteria, and say what to do when they disagree

# 1 · What this adds {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Every session so far had a $y$

| Session | The question |
|---|---|
| **02–03** | given $y$ and $X$, what is $\hat\beta$, and how sure are we? |
| **04–05** | given $y$, how well can we predict it, and how do we tune? |
| **06–07** | given a binary $y$, where do we set the threshold? |

::: {.warn}
All of it was **supervised**. There was always an outcome telling you what to look for.
:::

## Today there is no $y$

> The question is about the **structure of $X$ itself**.

::: {.tight}
- You have 200 macro series. They visibly move together
- Nobody labelled which of them matter, because there is nothing yet to matter *for*
- The question is: **how many distinct things are being measured?**
:::

::: {.check}
This is not a detour. Once you can compress 200 series into 3 factors, you can put those 3 factors
into any of the supervised methods from Sessions 03–07 — and that is what a *diffusion index* is.
:::

## The connection you should be looking for

::: {.step}
Session 05 shrank coefficients along the SVD basis of $X$, damping small-$d_j$ directions smoothly.
:::

::: {.step}
Today we **truncate** exactly those directions — keep the first $k$, discard the rest.
:::

::: {.check}
Principal components regression is, in this light, a **hard-thresholded ridge**. Same basis,
different rule. Keep that sentence for the end of Section 3.
:::

# 2 · PCA as maximisation {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The problem

Let $X$ be $n \times p$, columns **centred and standardised**. Find the unit vector maximising the
variance of the projection:

$$v_1 = \arg\max_{\|v\| = 1} v^\top \hat\Sigma v, \qquad \hat\Sigma = \tfrac1n X^\top X$$

::: {.warn}
Standardisation is **not optional**. Without it, whichever series is measured in the largest units
becomes "the first factor". PCA has no idea what a euro is.
:::

## Solve it: two lines of Lagrangian

$$\mathcal{L} = v^\top\hat\Sigma v - \phi(v^\top v - 1)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat\Sigma v = \phi v$$

::: {.step}
So $v$ **must be an eigenvector** of $\hat\Sigma$. And the objective evaluated at an eigenvector is
its own eigenvalue — so take the **largest** one.
:::

Subsequent components solve the same problem subject to orthogonality to those already found. You
get the eigenvectors in decreasing eigenvalue order.

::: {.check}
PCA is not an algorithm someone invented. It is the **solution** to a one-line optimisation problem.
:::

## Do it by hand, once

$$\hat\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}
\;\Longrightarrow\; \phi_1 = 3,\ v_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\binom{1}{1};
\quad \phi_2 = 1,\ v_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\binom{1}{-1}$$

::: {.step}
First component explains $3/(3+1) = 75\%$ of the variance. Its loading is $(1,1)$: **the average of
the two series**. The second is their difference.
:::

::: {.check}
Thirty seconds of arithmetic, and PCA stops being magic. This is a midterm question.
:::

## What that looks like on real series

```{python}
pair = ["elec_price_eur_kwh", "elec_price_incl_tax"]
A = Zdf[pair].to_numpy()
w, v = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(A.T))
order = np.argsort(w)[::-1]; w, v = w[order], v[:, order]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.1))
ax.scatter(A[:, 0], A[:, 1], s=13, color=CL.muted, alpha=.55, edgecolor="none")
for k, (c, lab) in enumerate([(CL.accent, "PC1"), (CL.warn, "PC2")]):
    d_ = v[:, k] * 2.4 * np.sqrt(w[k])
    ax.annotate("", xy=d_, xytext=-d_,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=c, lw=2.4))
    ax.text(d_[0] * 1.10, d_[1] * 1.10, f"{lab}\n{w[k]/w.sum():.0%} of variance",
            color=c, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="600", ha="center")
proj = (A @ v[:, [0]]) @ v[:, [0]].T
sub = np.random.default_rng(1).choice(len(A), 40, replace=False)
for i in sub:
    ax.plot([A[i, 0], proj[i, 0]], [A[i, 1], proj[i, 1]], color=CL.line, lw=.8, zorder=1)
ax.set_xlabel("electricity price, standardised")
ax.set_ylabel("price incl. tax, standardised")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
```

::: {.muted}
Thin grey lines are what PC1 throws away. Two series, one thing happening: the *level* of energy
prices in that country-year.
:::

# 3 · The SVD {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What software actually computes

With $X = UDV^\top$:

$$\hat\Sigma = \tfrac1n V D^2 V^\top, \qquad
\underbrace{V}_{\text{loadings}}, \qquad
\underbrace{Z = XV = UD}_{\text{scores}}, \qquad
\underbrace{\frac{d_j^2}{\sum_k d_k^2}}_{\text{variance share}}$$

::: {.step}
No covariance matrix is ever formed. Forming $X^\top X$ squares the condition number — Session 02's
warning, and the reason `numpy.linalg.svd` is the right entry point.
:::

## Eckart–Young

**Theorem.** Among all matrices of rank $\le k$, the one minimising $\|X - \tilde X\|_F$ is the
truncated SVD $\tilde X_k = U_k D_k V_k^\top$, and

$$\min_{\mathrm{rank}(\tilde X)\le k}\|X - \tilde X\|_F = \Big(\sum_{j > k} d_j^2\Big)^{1/2}$$

::: {.check}
This is the **precise** sense in which "the first $k$ components capture the most information". And
it tells you exactly what you lost: the discarded singular values.
:::

## Check it on our panel

```{python}
#| echo: true
def reconstruct(k):
    """The rank-k truncated SVD of the standardised panel."""
    return (U[:, :k] * D[:k]) @ Vt[:k]

for k in (1, 2, 3, 5):
    actual = np.linalg.norm(Z - reconstruct(k))
    theory = np.sqrt((D[k:]**2).sum())
    print(f"k={k}:  ||X - Xk||_F = {actual:7.3f}   sqrt(sum d_j^2, j>k) = {theory:7.3f}")
```

::: {.muted}
Identical to three decimals, as the theorem requires. When a formula and a computation agree to
machine precision, you have understood both.
:::

## The scree plot, and its elbow

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.7, 2.9))
kk = np.arange(1, min(11, len(VAR) + 1))

ax = axes[0]
ax.bar(kk, VAR[:len(kk)] * 100, color=[CL.accent if i < 3 else CL.muted for i in range(len(kk))],
       width=.62)
ax.plot(kk, VAR[:len(kk)] * 100, "o-", color=CL.ink, lw=1.3, ms=3.5)
ax.annotate("elbow", xy=(3.4, VAR[3] * 100 + 1), xytext=(6, 26), fontsize=9,
            color=CL.warn, fontweight="600",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=CL.warn, lw=1.4))
ax.set_xlabel("component"); ax.set_ylabel("% of variance")

ax = axes[1]
cum = np.cumsum(VAR) * 100
ax.plot(kk, cum[:len(kk)], "o-", color=CL.accent, lw=2.3, ms=4)
for lev, c in [(80, CL.good), (90, CL.muted)]:
    ax.axhline(lev, color=c, ls=":", lw=1.3)
    ax.text(9.4, lev + 1, f"{lev}%", color=c, fontsize=8)
ax.axvline(3, color=CL.warn, ls="--", lw=1.4)
ax.text(3.2, 42, f"3 components\n{cum[2]:.0f}%", color=CL.warn, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="600")
ax.set_xlabel("components retained"); ax.set_ylabel("cumulative % of variance")
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
Thirteen standardised indicators. Three components carry **83%** of the total variance; the fourth
adds eight more, and everything after it is under five.
:::

## Ridge damps; PCA truncates

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
dj = np.linspace(0.05, 4.0, 400)
LAM = 0.9
ax.plot(dj, dj**2 / (dj**2 + LAM), color=CL.accent, lw=2.6, label=r"ridge: $d_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda)$")
cut = 1.4
ax.plot(dj, (dj >= cut).astype(float), color=CL.warn, lw=2.6, ls="--",
        label="PCR: keep or discard")
ax.axvline(cut, color=CL.warn, ls=":", lw=1.1)
ax.text(cut + .06, .45, "truncation\npoint", color=CL.warn, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel(r"singular value  $d_j$   (how much the data vary in that direction)")
ax.set_ylabel("weight given to the direction")
ax.set_ylim(-.05, 1.12); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
**Same basis, different rule.** Ridge applies a smooth weight; principal components regression
applies a step function. Principal components regression is a hard-thresholded ridge.
:::

## The loadings tell you what a factor *is*

```{python}
K = 4
L = pd.DataFrame(Vt[:K].T, index=IND, columns=[f"PC{i+1}" for i in range(K)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
im = ax.imshow(L.to_numpy(), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-.6, vmax=.6, aspect="auto")
ax.set_xticks(range(K)); ax.set_xticklabels(L.columns, fontsize=9)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(IND)))
ax.set_yticklabels([c[:22] for c in IND], fontsize=7.5)
for i in range(len(IND)):
    for j in range(K):
        val = L.iloc[i, j]
        if abs(val) > .28:
            ax.text(j, i, f"{val:+.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7,
                    color="white" if abs(val) > .45 else CL.ink, fontweight="600")
ax.grid(visible=False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.muted}
Read down a column: which series move together. That is all a factor is — a weighted average of
series that happen to co-move.
:::

# 4 · Why more series helps {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The approximate factor model

Stock and Watson: a large macro panel is a few common shocks plus idiosyncratic noise.

$$X_{it} = \lambda_i^\top F_t + e_{it}, \qquad i = 1,\dots,N; \quad t = 1,\dots,T$$

::: {.step}
$F_t \in \mathbb{R}^r$ are the common factors; $\lambda_i$ the loadings. The **approximate** version
(Chamberlain–Rothschild) allows weak cross-sectional and serial correlation in $e_{it}$ — which is
what makes it usable on real data.
:::

## The result that should surprise you

::: {.step}
The principal-component estimator $\hat F_t$ is consistent for the **space spanned by** $F_t$ as
**both** $N \to \infty$ and $T \to \infty$, at rate $\min(\sqrt N, \sqrt T)$.
:::

::: {.check}
And if $\sqrt T / N \to 0$, the estimated factors can be treated as **known** in a second-stage
regression. The generated-regressor problem simply vanishes.
:::

::: {.warn}
**More series genuinely helps.** That is the opposite of everything Sessions 05 and 06 taught you.
Why?
:::

## Both effects, side by side

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
Ns_f = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]
Ns_r = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
T_ = 120

rec = []
for N in Ns_f:
    r = []
    for _ in range(30):
        F = rng.normal(size=T_)
        lam = rng.normal(1, .3, N)
        Xs = np.outer(F, lam) + rng.normal(0, 2.0, (T_, N))
        Fh = PCA(n_components=1).fit_transform((Xs - Xs.mean(0)) / Xs.std(0)).ravel()
        r.append(abs(np.corrcoef(Fh, F)[0, 1]))
    rec.append(np.mean(r))

err = []
for P_ in Ns_r:
    e = []
    for _ in range(30):
        Xa, Xb = rng.normal(size=(60, P_)), rng.normal(size=(400, P_))
        b = np.zeros(P_); b[0] = 1.0
        ya = Xa @ b + rng.normal(0, 1, 60)
        yb = Xb @ b + rng.normal(0, 1, 400)
        mm = LinearRegression().fit(Xa, ya)
        e.append(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yb, mm.predict(Xb))))
    err.append(np.mean(e))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.7, 2.9))
ax = axes[0]
ax.semilogx(Ns_f, rec, "o-", color=CL.good, lw=2.5, ms=5, base=2)
ax.set_xlabel("N — number of noisy series measuring ONE latent factor")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$|\mathrm{corr}(\hat F, F)|$")
ax.set_title("factor estimation: more is better", fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_ylim(.4, 1.03)

ax = axes[1]
ax.semilogx(Ns_r, err, "s-", color=CL.warn, lw=2.5, ms=5, base=2)
ax.set_xlabel("p — number of predictors, only the first of which matters")
ax.set_ylabel("test RMSE")
ax.set_title("regression: more is worse", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

::: {.check}
Left: each extra series is another **measurement of the same thing**, so its noise averages away.
Right: each extra predictor is another **free parameter**, so its noise is fitted.
:::

## Say the distinction out loud

::: {.step}
Sessions 05–06: an extra column is an extra **coefficient to estimate**. Variance goes up.
:::

::: {.step}
Session 08: an extra column is an extra **noisy reading of a latent quantity**. Averaging drives its
noise down like $1/\sqrt N$.
:::

::: {.warn}
Same table, opposite conclusion — because the *object being estimated* is different. This is the
best question of the semester, and the answer is "what are you estimating?"
:::

## Normalisation is a choice, not a discovery

To pin down the rotation we impose $F^\top F / T = I_r$ and $\Lambda^\top\Lambda$ diagonal.

::: {.warn}
Factors are identified **only up to rotation**. So *"Factor 1 is the business cycle"* is an
interpretation you are offering, never an estimate you have produced.
:::

::: {.check}
Write that caveat into your paper before you write the interpretation. A referee who finds the
interpretation without the caveat will not read further.
:::

# 5 · How many factors? {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Four answers, and they will disagree

::: {.tight}
- **Scree plot** — look for the elbow. Informal, often ambiguous
- **Cumulative variance** — retain 80–90%. Arbitrary but transparent
- **Bai–Ng information criteria** — $IC_{p1}, IC_{p2}, IC_{p3}$, with penalties that must vanish
  slower than $\min(N,T)^{-1}$
- **Ahn–Horenstein eigenvalue ratio** — $\hat r = \arg\max_k d_k / d_{k+1}$
:::

$$IC_{p1}(k) = \log V(k, \hat F^k) + k\left(\frac{N+T}{NT}\right)\log\left(\frac{NT}{N+T}\right)$$

## Compute all of them and look

```{python}
#| echo: true
N_, T_p = NIND, NOBS          # N series, T observations
def V(k):
    """Average residual sum of squares from a k-factor fit."""
    return ((Z - reconstruct(k))**2).mean()

c = (N_ + T_p) / (N_ * T_p)
ks = np.arange(1, 9)
ic1 = [np.log(V(k)) + k * c * np.log(1 / c) for k in ks]
ic2 = [np.log(V(k)) + k * c * np.log(min(N_, T_p)) for k in ks]
ic3 = [np.log(V(k)) + k * np.log(min(N_, T_p)) / min(N_, T_p) for k in ks]
ahr = [D[k - 1] / D[k] for k in ks]

print(f"N = {N_} series, T = {T_p} observations")
print(f"Bai-Ng IC_p1 minimised at k = {ks[int(np.argmin(ic1))]}"
      f"   Ahn-Horenstein argmax at k = {ks[int(np.argmax(ahr))]}")
print(f"cumulative variance: 3 components = {np.cumsum(VAR)[2]:.1%}")
```

## Look at what happened

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.7, 2.9))
ax = axes[0]
for v, c_, lab in [(ic1, CL.accent, r"$IC_{p1}$"), (ic2, CL.good, r"$IC_{p2}$"),
                   (ic3, CL.warn, r"$IC_{p3}$")]:
    ax.plot(ks, v, "o-", color=c_, lw=2.0, ms=4, label=lab)
ax.set_xlabel("number of factors k"); ax.set_ylabel("information criterion")
ax.set_title("Bai–Ng: still falling at k = 8", fontsize=9.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=8)

ax = axes[1]
ax.bar(ks, ahr, color=[CL.warn if k == ks[int(np.argmax(ahr))] else CL.muted for k in ks],
       width=.62)
ax.axhline(1, color=CL.line, lw=1.0)
ax.set_xlabel("k"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$d_k / d_{k+1}$")
ax.set_title("Ahn–Horenstein: peaks at k = 5", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
Scree says 3. Cumulative variance says 3. Ahn–Horenstein says 5. Bai–Ng is still falling at 8.
:::

## Why Bai–Ng failed here, and what to do

::: {.step}
Bai–Ng is consistent as **both** $N$ and $T$ grow. We have $T = 239$ observations but only
$N = 13$ series. The penalty $\frac{N+T}{NT}\log\frac{NT}{N+T}$ is tiny when $N$ is small, so it
never bites.
:::

::: {.check}
Which is not a failure of the criterion. It is the criterion **telling you** your panel is not wide
enough for it. Report all four numbers, say they disagree, and say which one your $N$ and $T$
support.
:::

::: {.warn}
What loses marks: reporting one criterion, the one that gave the number you wanted.
:::

# 6 · Diffusion-index forecasting {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Two stages

::: {.step}
**1.** Extract $\hat F_t$ by PCA from the standardised, stationary panel of $N$ series.
:::

::: {.step}
**2.** Forecast the target with a small regression on the factors and a few own lags:

$$\hat y_{t+h} = \hat\alpha + \sum_{j=1}^{r}\hat\beta_j \hat F_{jt}
+ \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\hat\gamma_\ell\, y_{t-\ell}$$
:::

::: {.check}
Two hundred series enter stage 1. Three numbers leave it. Stage 2 is an ordinary regression you
already know how to diagnose.
:::

## The rule you must not break

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 2.9))
YR = list(range(2011, 2024))
for i, cut in enumerate([2017, 2018, 2019, 2020]):
    yb = 3 - i
    tr = [t for t in YR if t < cut]
    ax.barh(yb, len(tr), left=0, height=.55, color=CL.accent, alpha=.85)
    ax.barh(yb, 1, left=len(tr), height=.55, color=CL.warn)
    ax.text(-0.4, yb, f"origin {cut}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.text(len(tr) / 2, yb, "PCA fitted here", ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=7.5, color="white", fontweight="600")
    ax.text(len(tr) + 1.25, yb, "predict", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=CL.warn,
            fontweight="600")
ax.set_xlim(-3.4, len(YR) + 1)
ax.set_ylim(-.6, 3.7)
ax.set_xlabel("years of the panel used")
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(visible=False)
for s in ("left", "bottom"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.warn}
Factors must be **re-estimated at every forecast origin**, from data available at that time.
Extracting from the full sample and then backtesting is look-ahead bias, and it is the single most
common flaw in student factor-model projects.
:::

## Measure the leak on our panel

```{python}
#| echo: true
def diffusion_rmse(target, R=3, leaky=False, first=6):
    dd = panel.copy()
    dd["yn"] = dd.groupby("geo")[target].shift(-1)
    dd = dd.dropna(subset=["yn"])
    if leaky:                                    # WRONG: PCA sees the whole sample
        Zf = (dd[IND] - dd[IND].mean()) / dd[IND].std()
        Fall = PCA(n_components=R).fit_transform(Zf)
    num = den = 0
    for t in sorted(dd.time.unique())[first:]:
        tr, te = (dd.time < t).to_numpy(), (dd.time == t).to_numpy()
        if leaky:
            Ftr, Fte = Fall[tr], Fall[te]
        else:                                    # RIGHT: refit PCA on the past only
            mu, sd = dd.loc[tr, IND].mean(), dd.loc[tr, IND].std()
            p = PCA(n_components=R).fit((dd.loc[tr, IND] - mu) / sd)
            Ftr = p.transform((dd.loc[tr, IND] - mu) / sd)
            Fte = p.transform((dd.loc[te, IND] - mu) / sd)
        b = LinearRegression().fit(Ftr, dd.loc[tr, "yn"])
        num += ((dd.loc[te, "yn"] - b.predict(Fte))**2).sum(); den += te.sum()
    return np.sqrt(num / den)

lk = diffusion_rmse("elec_price_eur_kwh", leaky=True)
hn = diffusion_rmse("elec_price_eur_kwh", leaky=False)
print(f"factors from the full sample : RMSE {lk:.4f}")
print(f"factors refitted each origin : RMSE {hn:.4f}      ratio {lk/hn:.3f}")
```

## Be honest about that number

::: {.step}
On **this** panel the leak buys about 2%. The factor space is stable across thirteen years, so
knowing the future rotation tells you almost nothing.
:::

::: {.warn}
That is not a licence. You cannot know in advance whether the leak is worth 2% or 40% — and it is
40% exactly when the factor structure shifts, which is the case you most want to forecast.
:::

::: {.check}
The discipline is justified by the fact that **you cannot audit it after the fact**, not by the size
of the measured gap on one dataset.
:::

# 7 · Takeaways {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Key takeaways

::: {.tight}
1. PCA is the **solution** to a constrained maximisation — hence eigenvectors, hence the SVD
2. Eckart–Young says truncation is optimal, and names what you discarded
3. Ridge damps the small-$d_j$ directions; PCR truncates them. Same basis
4. More series **help** factor estimation because each is another reading of one object
5. Factors are identified only up to rotation — interpretation is a claim, not an estimate
6. Re-estimate factors at every forecast origin. Every time
:::

## What loses marks

::: {.tight}
- Running PCA on **unstandardised** columns
- Naming a factor ("this is the business cycle") without the rotation caveat
- Reporting one factor-count criterion out of four
- Extracting factors once on the full sample, then backtesting
- Reporting "80% of variance explained" as if 80% were a rule rather than a choice
:::

## Now, the practice

::: {.get}
Ninety minutes, in your groups. You will extract factors from a wide panel, defend the number you
retained against at least three criteria, and build a diffusion-index forecast whose factors are
re-estimated at every origin.
:::
